title: Special-coset representatives in a rational immediate analytic field
statement: Let $k\subseteq K$ be complete fields with compatible nontrivial nonarchimedean real absolute values, with $k$ algebraically closed [def-weil-field]. Put $F^\circ=\{x\in F:|x|\le1\}$ [def-trf-valuation-ring], $\widetilde F=F^\circ/\{x:|x|<1\}$ and $\Gamma_F=|F^\times|$ for $F=k,K$. Assume $\widetilde K=\widetilde k$ and $\Gamma_K=\Gamma_k$. For $u\in K$ let $k(u)^\wedge$ be the closure of the subfield generated by $k$ and $u$. Assume $K=k(z)^\wedge$ for some $z\in K\setminus k$, and let $p=\operatorname{char}\widetilde k>0$. For a field $F$ with this absolute value, $a\in F$ and $s>0$, put $S_{a,s}(F)=\{c^p-ac+e:c,e\in F,\ |pc^p|<s,\ |e|<s\}$. A coset $b+S_{a,s}(F)$ is special if it does not contain zero, the infimum of the absolute values of its elements is $s$, and either $a=0$ or $(a,s)=(1,1)$. For every special coset $b+S_{a,s}(K)$, there exists $v\in b+S_{a,s}(K)$ such that either $v\in k$ or $K=k(v)^\wedge$.

source.place: Proposition 6.2.4, type 4 case, printed p. 42, with the finite moderately ramified extension equal to K itself; proof printed pp. 47–48.

proof.text: Put $C=b+S_{a,s}(K)$, $S=S_{a,s}(K)$ and $q=|p|<1$. Here $p$ is prime because it is a positive field characteristic, and $|n|\le1$ for every integer $n$. The binomial formula shows that $S$ is an additive subgroup: if $q|c|^p,q|d|^p<s$, then $q|c+d|^p<s$ and $|(c+d)^p-c^p-d^p|\le q\max(|c|^p,|d|^p)<s$, since every intermediate binomial coefficient is divisible by $p$. This error is absorbed into the allowed $e$-term. Negation is the same calculation with $d=-c$, and $0\in S$. In particular the ball $\{e:|e|<s\}$ lies in $S$, and $x+S=C$ for any $x\in C$.

source.place: Definition of S and cosets before Lemma 6.1.2, printed p. 37; binomial calculation expanded.

proof.text: Every $x\in C$ satisfies $|px|<s$. If $q=0$ this is immediate. If $q>0$, first note $|pu|<s$ for every $u=c^p-ac+e\in S$: the first and third summands have this bound by definition; the middle is zero when $a=0$, and when $a=1,s=1$ it has norm $q|c|=q^{1-1/p}(q|c|^p)^{1/p}<1$. Since $\inf|C|=s$ and $q<1$, choose $x_0\in C$ with $|x_0|<s/q$. For any $x\in C$, the previous subgroup calculation gives $x-x_0\in S$, and $|px|\le\max(|px_0|,|p(x-x_0)|)<s$. Thus this bound remains available after each change of representative.

source.place: Lemma 6.1.2(i), printed p. 37; the needed bound is proved directly for the two special normalizations.

proof.text: The number $r=\inf_{c\in k}|z-c|$ is positive and not attained. If it were zero, approximations $c_n\to z$ would be Cauchy in the complete field $k$, putting $z\in k$. If $|z-c|=r>0$, choose $t\in k$ with $|t|=r$ using $\Gamma_K=\Gamma_k$, and lift the residue of $(z-c)/t$ to $d\in k^\circ$ using $\widetilde K=\widetilde k$. Then $|z-c-td|<r$, a contradiction. Algebraic closedness also makes $z$ transcendental over $k$. Translations $w=z-\beta$, $\beta\in k$, preserve $k[z]=k[w]$, $k(z)^\wedge=k(w)^\wedge$ and this same positive, unattained distance $r$.

source.place: Type 4 discussion preceding Lemma 6.2.7, printed p. 44; immediacy argument written out.

proof.text: Polynomials in $z$ are dense in $K$. Indeed, for $\alpha\in k$, choose $\beta\in k$ with $|z-\beta|<|z-\alpha|$, possible by nonattainment. With $t=(z-\beta)/(\beta-\alpha)$ we have $|t|<1$ and $z-\alpha=(\beta-\alpha)(1+t)$. The polynomial $Q_N(z)=(\beta-\alpha)^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N}(-t)^j$ satisfies $|1/(z-\alpha)-Q_N(z)|=|\beta-\alpha|^{-1}|t|^{N+1}\to0$. Every rational function in $z$ is a finite sum of polynomials and scalar multiples of powers of such inverses, by factorization of its denominator over $k$. Approximating these finitely many factors gives polynomial approximations, and $k(z)$ is dense in $K$ by hypothesis. Choose $x\in k[z]$ with $|x-b|<s$; then $x\in C$. Among the nonzero polynomials with value in $C$, choose one of smallest degree $m$. They are nonzero since $0\notin C$.

source.place: Paragraph before Lemma 6.2.7, p. 44, and type 4 proof of Proposition 6.2.4, p. 47; polynomial approximation expanded by finite geometric sums.

proof.text: If $m>1$, normalize the chosen polynomial by translation. Factor it as $P(T)=A\prod_{j=1}^{m}(T-\alpha_j)$ over $k$. Choose $\beta\in k$ with $|z-\beta|<\min_j|z-\alpha_j|$. Put $w=z-\beta$ and $P(w+\beta)=\sum_{i=0}^m b_iw^i$. Then $|\beta-\alpha_j|=|z-\alpha_j|>|w|$. Expanding the finite product, each contribution to $b_iw^i$ is bounded by $|A|\prod_j|\beta-\alpha_j|=|P(z)|=|x|$, so $|p b_i w^i|\le|px|<s$ for every $i$. The degree is still $m$ and $b_m=A\ne0$. This normalization changes the coordinate, not $x$ or $C$, and $r=\inf_{c\in k}|w-c|$ remains unchanged.

source.place: Type 4 proof of Proposition 6.2.4, printed p. 47; the invertibility/termwise-bound step is proved by the displayed factorization.

proof.text: Assume $m>1$ and $p\nmid m$. Apply [lem-trf-analytic-special-coset-leading-bound] to the normalized coordinate $w$, the same special coset $x+S=C$ and coefficients $b_i$. Completeness, algebraic closedness, immediacy and $K=k(w)^\wedge$ hold; the additional $a=1$ coefficient bounds hold by the preceding step, since then $s=1$. The strict conclusion is $|b_m|r^m<s$. Choose $c_0\in k$ with $|b_m||w-c_0|^m<s$, using the definition of $r$ and continuity of the power function. The element $d=b_m(w-c_0)^m$ has $|d|<s$, so $x-d\in C$. Its leading coefficient cancels that of $x$, giving a polynomial of degree less than $m$, contradicting minimality. (It cannot be the zero polynomial since $0\notin C$.)

source.place: Lemma 6.2.9, pp. 45–47, applied in the proof of Proposition 6.2.4, printed p. 47.

proof.text: Assume instead $m>1$ and $p\mid m$. Algebraic closedness of $k$ supplies $h\in k$ with $h^p=b_m$ in both equal and mixed characteristic. Set $c=h w^{m/p}$. The coefficient bound gives $|pc^p|=|p b_m w^m|<s$, so $c^p-ac\in S$. Hence $x-c^p+ac\in C$ by the subgroup calculation. Its degree is strictly less than $m$: $c^p=b_m w^m$ cancels the leading term, and $ac$ is zero for $a=0$ or has degree $m/p<m$ for $a=1$. This again contradicts minimality. Thus $m\le1$. If $m=0$, take $v=x\in k$. If $m=1$, write $v=x=Az+B$ with $A\in k^\times,B\in k$; then $z=(v-B)/A$, so $k(v)=k(z)$ and their closures are equal to $K$. In each case $v\in C$, as required.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 6.2.4, printed pp. 47–48; the exact p-th root in algebraically closed k handles both characteristic cases.

An algebraically closed k with K of type 4 falls under 6.2.1(ii), and L=K. The item statement is unchanged and matches the source hypothesis by hypothesis. The new node lem-trf-analytic-special-coset-leading-bound matches Lemma 6.2.9 exactly (p∤m, m≥1, the a=1 bound |p b_i z^i|<1 for i≥1, ≤ in general and < for m>1). I checked that the source's initial shift |pz|<r keeps that a=1 hypothesis (|γ|=|z|, |z'|<|z|), so the node holds for an arbitrary z. Small case m=1, b=z gives r≤s, which is consistent. Steps: (1) subgroup via binomial divisibility, including negation for p=2; (2) |px|<s, both q=0 and q>0, including q|c|<1 when a=1; (3) r>0 and not attained, using equal value groups and residue fields, and z transcendental; (4) explicit geometric-series approximation and partial fractions show k[z] is dense, so a least-degree representative exists and is nonzero; (5) the translation normalization bounds each monomial by |A|∏|β-α_j|=|x|, which gives the node's a=1 hypothesis; (6) the strict bound of the node gives c_0 with |b_m(w-c_0)^m|<s, lowering the degree; (7) since k is algebraically closed there is an exact p-th root, ac has degree m/p, and the endpoints m=0 and m=1 give v in k or k(v)=k(z). Each step is elementary apart from the one node citation. The node satisfies B1-B7, has no dependencies and no cycle, and is strictly smaller than the item (D1/D2 ok).
